Our first customer asked for a refund on day three.

I said yes before they finished the sentence.

A week later they came back and bought the annual plan, and told two colleagues. I used to think refunds were a loss. Now I think of them as the cheapest way to learn what the product still gets wrong.

What did your last refund teach you?

I rewrote our onboarding email four times.

The fourth version was eleven words long.

It had the best reply rate we have ever measured. Not because it was clever, but because it asked exactly one question and nothing else. Every extra sentence I removed made the answer easier to give.

Short is a kindness.

We stopped holding Monday status meetings.

Instead, everyone writes three lines on Friday afternoon: what shipped, what is stuck, what is next.

The team got back four hours a week each. More importantly, the stuck list now gets read by someone who can help. A meeting asks for attention. A note asks for a decision.

Try one quiet week.

A customer called to say our invoice was confusing.

It had been confusing for two years. Nobody had told us.

That afternoon we cut it from twenty lines to six. Support tickets about billing dropped by half the following month. Most of your friction is invisible until someone is kind enough to point at it.

Ask for the complaint you are not hearing.

I used to apologise at the start of every email.

Sorry to bother you. Sorry for the delay. Sorry if this is a silly question.

Then I counted: eleven apologies in one working day. I deleted them all and the emails got shorter, clearer and, oddly, warmer. People answered faster when I stopped asking permission to be answered.

Say the thing.
